headline: Buses and the Climate Card

elements.old: A graphic-design decision doing policy work — it made a complex network legible at a glance.
peak gain in bus travel speed

elements.new: fewer bus accidents in the first year

elements.old:
July 2004: distance-based fares with free transfers across modes — buses and subway
unified for the first time. Ridership estimates range +9% to +21% depending on baseline.
elements.new:
July 2004: fares by distance, free transfers between bus and subway
Ridership up 9% to 21%, depending on the years compared

elements.old: City and town buses, including late-night

elements.new: Planned: Hangang River Bus, self-driving buses

elements.old:
Break-even is about four rides a day — set deliberately so the

elements.new:
Pilot January 2024 · full launch July 2024
₩62,000 without bikes · youth: ₩58,000 with bikes

elements.old: Same mechanism as OMNY fare capping. Completely different meaning — riding becomes a civic act, not a transaction.
elements.new: New York today: OMNY fare capping · Citi Bike sold separately

movedToNotes: The whole bus network switched over in one night in July 2004. The fare system later spread to Gyeonggi (2007) and Incheon (2009).
Main road speeds rose 33 to 50% (December 2004). Research linked to UN-Habitat calls the 24% drop in bus accidents the reform's biggest success.
Ridership estimates run from about 9% to 21% depending on the years compared. Never add them together; UN-Habitat's cautious figure is about 9% (406,000 more daily riders).
UN-Habitat said the reform "considerably increased overall service quality." The city still paid high subsidies in the first few years.
The four colors (blue, green, red, yellow) made a complicated network easy to read. A graphic design choice helped the policy work.
Climate Card was announced in September 2023; ₩65,000 a month includes Ttareungi bikes. Not covered: Shinbundang Line, buses licensed outside Seoul, metropolitan express buses.
If asked: the River Bus is an add-on at ₩67,000. It is not in the base ₩65,000 card.
Each reload is one top-up of the pass (usually 30 days), so the same person is counted many times. Seoul hasn't released user counts or how much driving it replaced.
Fare capping: once you pay for a set number of rides in any 7 days, the rest of your rides in those 7 days are free.
New York has a similar idea in OMNY fare capping. Seoul named its pass for the climate and added bike share, so the city presents riding as part of its climate plan.
If asked about break-even: "₩65,000 is about the price of 42 subway rides at ₩1,550."

movedToNotes: Row 01: organics (food and yard waste) were 1.4% of residential waste in 2024 and 2.4% in 2025.
Row 01: only about 17% of NYC trash is recycled, composted or reused. DSNY says up to 75% is possible.
Row 01: Fines April 2025, paused in 3 weeks, back January 1, 2026.
Row 01: the Independent Budget Office (IBO) found that food waste pickup nearly tripled while fines were on, then fell about 43% after they stopped.
Row 01: NYC bins don't show you what you threw out, and there's no reward for cutting back.
Row 01: Refuse rooms are already required, so bins that weigh food waste belong in the building code.

Row 02: my main recommendation. Slow down here. LL97 sets the target and the fine but leaves the financing to owners. About 11% of buildings are over the 2024 to 2029 limits, and about 63% would be over the 2030 limits if nothing changes.
Row 02: LL97 covers buildings over 25,000 sq ft. The 63% is a projection if owners do nothing more.
Row 03: the problems are code, permitting and landlord consent. The technology is ready.
Row 03, three asks: an approved-kit list, an easy permit, and a renter's right to install.
Row 03: Department of Buildings (DOB) should let you plug one in without filing for a full alteration permit.
Row 03: Germany's balcony solar boom shows it scales once permits are simple.
Row 04, two asks: add Citi Bike to one OMNY pass, and name it for the climate.
Row 04: OMNY fare capping is a similar idea (explained on slide 18).
Row 05: High Line was an old rail line. Cheonggyecheon and Seoullo were roads people drove on.
Row 05: Cross Bronx plans would build a deck with parks over the sunken highway (called a cap). BQE is the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway.
Row 05: the gridlock opponents predicted did not happen.
At 2:55, hold all five rows on screen and move to the close.

headline: Carrot and Stick Compared

elements.old: Seoul proved the carrot works at scale.
2 million TOE six months early. 1.68 million people enrolled voluntarily. Retrofits financed at 1.75%.
elements.new: 2 million TOE goal met six months early · 1.68 million Eco-Mileage participants · retrofit loans at 1.75%

elements.old: Seoul also proved the carrot has a ceiling.
It banned landfilling, failed to build the replacement, and the waste went 130 km to communities that didn't make it.
elements.new: Direct landfill ban from January 2026 · not enough incinerators · some trash sent about 130 km by road

elements.old: New York is running the opposite experiment.
The stick without the carrot — and about 63% of its buildings are projected to miss their 2030 caps.
elements.new: LL97 fines $268 per ton over the limit · financing left to owners · about 63% would miss 2030 limits if nothing changes

elements.old:
Mandates set the date. Money decides whether anyone can meet it.
Seoul and New York each built one half.
Full reference list in the submitted PDF.
elements.new: Full reference list in the submitted PDF.

movedToNotes: Seoul showed that incentives can work across a whole city.

Seoul also showed the limit. The landfill ban started before there were enough incinerators, so some trash now goes to private incinerators in Cheonan and Sejong, and Gangnam planned to send some to Cheongju.
New York is doing the reverse, with fines and no city loans.
Closing line, say as written: "If I had to pick one idea for New York, it would be the retrofit loans. LL97 already has the fines, and owners still need a way to pay for the work."
Distances, if asked: Cheonan about 85 km, Cheongju about 110 km, Sejong about 125 km in a straight line. The 130 km on the slide is the road distance reported by Seoul Economic Daily (October 2026).
Q&A: "Would you rather design under Seoul's loans or New York's fines?"
Q&A: "Seoul banned landfilling before it had enough incinerators. Is LL97 asking for retrofits faster than New York's workers and suppliers can do them?"
Q&A: "Lotte World Tower is LEED Gold at 123 floors. Nowon was designed for zero energy at 121 units. Which one does more for the climate?"
If asked about Nowon: it targets net-zero energy and reports about 75 to 80% self-sufficiency. Avoid the 100% energy cost claim; use up to 61% lower.
Q&A: "Composting nearly tripled under fines and fell about 43% after the fines stopped. How do you add a reward so fines don't hit low-income families hardest?"
Q&A: "Should we count all park space, or only park space within a five-minute walk?"
Q&A: "Cheonggyecheon took out a highway that carried 168,000 vehicles a day and the predicted gridlock never came. Why is that hard to act on here?"
Mention the full source list is in the submitted PDF.
